2:
SAY:
- Read the cultural sensitivity statement aloud, in a calm voice.
- 'In this story we will read about the Coorong and the Ngarrindjeri Country it sits on.'
- 'Some of the language reflects the time it was written, not how we speak today.'

DO:
- Pause briefly so students take it in.
- Move on without inviting discussion.

TEACHER NOTES:
Deliver as a one-minute orientation at the start of the lesson. Not a discussion task.

SENSITIVITY ADVISORY:
- What it is: references to deceased persons, historical perspectives, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories and cultures.
- Framing language: see SAY.
- Watch for: students who may have personal or cultural connections; signs of discomfort during reading.
- Protocol: pause if a student is distressed, offer a quiet seat or water, let the student step out and rejoin without comment.

WATCH FOR:
- Body language at the moment of reading.

[Stage: Lesson Orientation]
7:
SAY:
- 'Today we are reading more of Storm Boy, learning two new words, and writing a Single Paragraph Outline - we call it an SPO - to summarise part of the story.'
- Read each Success Criterion aloud and point as you go.
- 'If SPOs feel new, that is okay. We will build it together.'

DO:
- Point to each SC.
- Tap the SPO criterion twice so students hold it as today's writing focus.

TEACHER NOTES:
The SPO criterion is what the booklet task assesses. Comprehension and vocab feed into the writing.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who cannot say the SPO goal back; they will need extra modelling at slides 30 to 32.

[Stage: LI and SC]
8:
SAY:
- 'On your desk: pencil, booklet and novel, mini whiteboard and texta.'
- 'Thumbs up when you are ready.'

DO:
- Scan for thumbs.

TEACHER NOTES:
Ready-to-learn check.

[Stage: Materials]
9:
SOURCES:
- Ochre Education Text Level Reading guide.

SAY:
- 'We are about to read more of Storm Boy. Listen and follow along.'

DO:
- Settle the class with novels open.

TEACHER NOTES:
Reading mode is teacher choice. Decide before the lesson.

[Stage: Text-Level Reading]
10:
SAY:
- 'We are reading pages 62 to 66 of Storm Boy now.'
- 'I will pause where I have marked. Listen for words that are new.'

DO:
- Pre-mark your novel with pause points and queries before the lesson.
- Read at a steady pace; pause where marked, ask a planned query, take 2 to 3 responses, keep reading.
- Note any vocabulary students flag.

TEACHER NOTES:
No handbook supplied to this notes pass. Confirm pause points using your Literature Study Guide before teaching.

WATCH FOR:
- Students losing the page.
- Trouble with multi-clause sentences in this section.

[Stage: Read-Aloud]
11:
SAY:
- 'Two new words from this part of the story. Listen and we will use them.'

DO:
- Display the slide and move on.

TEACHER NOTES:
Section divider. Today's words are shudder and feebly.

[Stage: Vocabulary]
12:
SOURCES:
- Macquarie Dictionary, 2024.

SAY:
- 'Watch this first.'
- 'The word is shudder. Say it with me. Shudder.'
- 'To shudder is to shake suddenly from fear or cold. It is a verb.'
- 'In Storm Boy, Storm Boy could feel the shock and shudder of the line as the water thundered round it.'
- Ask: 'Say shudder with me.' Expected: 'Shudder.'

DO:
- Demonstrate a quick shudder yourself - shoulders shake briefly.
- Run affixes: 'shuddered, shuddering'.
- Point to associations: shiver, shake, tremble.

TEACHER NOTES:
A shudder is sudden, not slow. Anchor on fear or cold as the cause.

WATCH FOR:
- Students confusing shudder with shutter (a window shutter).

[Stage: I Do | Vocabulary]
13:
SAY:
- 'Read with me. Anna felt a shudder as she stepped into the icy cold water at the beach.'
- Ask: 'On your whiteboards, draw a face that shows what Anna might look like. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask one student to act out the shudder.

WATCH FOR:
- Students drawing happy faces; remind them shudder is from fear or cold.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
14:
SAY:
- 'Two sentences. One uses shudder correctly.'
- 'Sentence one: Sara shuddered the door when she heard the thunder rumbling.'
- 'Sentence two: Sara felt a shudder when she heard the thunder rumbling in the distance.'
- Ask: 'Show me one or two. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 2.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why is sentence one wrong?'

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers 1 or 2
Script:
- 'Sentence one or sentence two? Show me.'
- Scan for: clear majority on 2.
PROCEED:
- Confirm 2 and explain shudder describes what the body does, not an action on something.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students think shudder works like shake (you can shake a door).
- Reteach with examples: 'You can shake a door. You cannot shudder a door.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students choosing 1 because they hear the action 'shuddered'.

[Stage: CFU | Vocabulary]
15:
SAY:
- 'Think of a time you have shuddered from the cold. Picture it.'
- 'When I tap the bell, silently act out your shudder.'

DO:
- Give 30 seconds of think time.
- Invite three or four volunteers to act.
- Ask: 'What told you that was a shudder?' Expected: tense face, quick shake, holding self.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who do not want to act; let them mime in their seat.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
16:
SAY:
- 'Write a sentence using shudder. Whiteboards. Three minutes.'
- 'When I click, an example will appear. Yours can be different.'

DO:
- Circulate; read 5 boards.
- Reveal: 'When the snowball hit Lily's neck, a sudden shudder went down her spine.'
- Cold call one student to share.

WATCH FOR:
- Students using shudder as a noun ('a shudder') and as a verb ('shuddered'); both are correct.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
17:
SAY:
- 'When you shudder, you do which of these? Show me on your fingers.'
- 'One: push something forcefully. Two: shut something quickly. Three: shake suddenly from fear or cold. Four: sway to and fro.'
- Ask: 'Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 3.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why three?'

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers 1-4
Script:
- 'Show me which one matches shudder.'
- Scan for: clear majority on 3.
PROCEED:
- Confirm 3 and review the meaning.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students choose sway because both involve movement.
- Reteach with the contrast: 'Sway is slow and side-to-side. Shudder is sudden and from fear or cold.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students confusing sway with shudder.

[Stage: CFU | Vocabulary]
18:
SOURCES:
- Macquarie Dictionary, 2024.

SAY:
- 'Watch this first.'
- 'The word is feebly. Say it with me. Feebly.'
- 'Feebly means weakly. It is an adverb - it tells us how something is done.'
- 'In Storm Boy, after being pulled onto shore, the man staggered feebly up the beach.'
- Ask: 'Say feebly with me.' Expected: 'Feebly.'

DO:
- Walk a few steps weakly to demonstrate.
- Run affixes: 'feeble' (the adjective).
- Point to associations: frail, weak.

TEACHER NOTES:
Feebly is an adverb (modifying a verb). The man staggered weakly.

WATCH FOR:
- Students mishearing feebly as freely; emphasise the b sound.

[Stage: I Do | Vocabulary]
19:
SAY:
- 'Read with me. The baby bird chirped feebly, too weak to make a loud sound.'
- Ask: 'On your whiteboards, draw a baby bird and show why it is chirping feebly.'

DO:
- Scan boards. Look for small, weak, sick or tired birds.
- Ask one student to explain their drawing.

WATCH FOR:
- Students drawing strong birds; redirect to weakly.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
20:
SAY:
- 'When you do something feebly, you do it weakly.'
- 'Think of a time you moved weakly. Picture it.'
- Ask: 'Tell your partner: when did you move feebly?'

DO:
- Time partner talk for 90 seconds.
- Cold call three students.
- Look for: tired after running, sick with a cold, lifting something heavy.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who default to the slide example; push for their own.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
21:
SAY:
- 'Build a sentence using feebly. Stem: Grandpa moved feebly while trying to help blank.'
- 'Whiteboards. Three minutes.'
- 'When I click, an example appears.'

DO:
- Circulate; read 5 boards.
- Reveal: 'lift the heavy moving box.'
- Cold call one student.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who write something Grandpa would do strongly; reinforce feebly means weakly.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
22:
SAY:
- 'Six words. Which have a similar meaning to feebly?'
- Ask: 'Whiteboards: list the matches. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: frail, weak, not strong, fragile.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why does strong not fit?'

WATCH FOR:
- Students writing strong because of association; redirect to the meaning.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
23:
SAY:
- 'Two pictures. Which dog is moving feebly?'
- Ask: 'Show me A or B. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask one student to defend their choice; look for 'because feebly means weakly'.

TEACHER NOTES:
The correct answer depends on the images on the slide - choose the dog that looks weak, slow or unsteady.

WATCH FOR:
- Students choosing the playful or jumping dog.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
24:
SAY:
- 'Three sentence stems with feebly. Complete each in your own words. Three minutes.'
- 'Stem one: The puppy barked feebly, but...'
- 'Stem two: The puppy barked feebly, so...'
- 'Stem three: The puppy barked feebly because...'

DO:
- Circulate; read several boards.
- Cold call three students - one for each stem.
- Reveal modelled completions and discuss.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Whiteboard Show + Cold Call
Script:
- 'Hold up your three completions.'
- Scan for: 80% have completions that match the meaning of feebly (weak, sick, tired puppy).
PROCEED:
- Move to the booklet task.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students complete stems with strong actions.
- Reteach with the rule: 'Feebly means weak. The rest of the sentence has to fit a weak puppy.'
- Re-check: 'Rewrite one stem so it fits feebly.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who use feebly as the only word and forget the conjunction.

[Stage: CFU | Vocabulary]
25:
SAY:
- 'Open your booklet to Lesson 17 Vocabulary.'
- 'Complete the tasks for shudder and feebly.'
- 'If a word feels new, look back at the slides.'

DO:
- Hand out booklets.
- Set timer.
- Circulate; read first 2 to 3 answers per student.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: pair with a peer to talk through one example for each word before writing.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: write one sentence that uses both shudder and feebly together.

TEACHER NOTES:
Flag students who cannot use either word in a sentence; they need extra modelling in the SPO segment.

WATCH FOR:
- Students copying examples from the slides.

[Stage: You Do | Vocabulary]
26:
SAY:
- 'Now we move to summarising. The skill today is taking a chunk of the story and turning it into a Single Paragraph Outline that captures the main ideas.'

DO:
- Display and move on.

TEACHER NOTES:
Section divider. The SPO is the writing focus and the booklet task at the end.

[Stage: Sentence-Level Writing]
27:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first.'
- 'A summary is a brief statement. It does not include extra details, just the main ideas.'
- 'Why summarise? To boost comprehension, focus on the main idea, retain information and analyse information.'
- 'I am going to model a summary of what we just read.'

DO:
- Point to each reason as you read it.
- Give a quick verbal summary of pages 62 to 66.

TEACHER NOTES:
Students often confuse summary with retelling. Emphasise main ideas only.

[Stage: I Do | SPO Purpose]
28:
SAY:
- 'Whiteboards. We will summarise this part of the story together.'
- 'I will use the question prompts: who, what doing, when, where, why, how.'
- Ask each prompt in turn; expected: students pair-share an answer.

DO:
- Time partner talk for 90 seconds per question, or do as a class brainstorm if time is short.
- Capture key answers on the board for the SPO later.

TEACHER NOTES:
This builds the raw material for the SPO. Keep answers visible.

WATCH FOR:
- Students retelling everything; pull them back to one short answer per question.

[Stage: We Do | Summarise]
29:
SAY:
- 'Big ideas from the story so far. Read with me.'
- Read each big idea chorally.
- Ask: 'Which big idea felt most important to you?'

DO:
- Choral read each big idea.
- Cold call three students.

TEACHER NOTES:
This frames Mr Percival as the hero of this section, which is the topic sentence focus that follows.

[Stage: We Do | Big Ideas]
30:
SAY:
- 'A Single Paragraph Outline puts your writing in an order that is easy for readers to understand.'
- 'Today we will build an SPO to summarise key ideas in Storm Boy.'
- 'Read along with me.'

DO:
- Choral read the slide.
- Point to the words 'topic sentence', 'supporting detail', 'concluding sentence'.

TEACHER NOTES:
Frames the SPO as a planning tool, not a paragraph.

[Stage: We Do | SPO Intro]
31:
SAY:
- 'A paragraph has three parts.'
- 'Topic sentence - it expresses the main idea.'
- 'Supporting details - they support the topic sentence.'
- 'Concluding sentence - it summarises, echoing the topic sentence without repeating word for word.'
- Ask: 'Listen for those three words: topic, support, conclude.'

DO:
- Point to each part as you read its meaning.
- Use a small finger gesture (top, middle, bottom) to anchor each part.

TEACHER NOTES:
This is the I Do for paragraph structure.

[Stage: I Do | Paragraph Parts]
32:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first. The topic sentence is given.'
- 'TS: Thanks to Mr Percival, they were able to work as a team to finally rescue the first man from the rickety boat.'
- 'I need to find three details from the story that support that idea.'
- 'I am going to leave them in note form, not full sentences.'

DO:
- Read the topic sentence aloud.
- Show the empty SPO frame.

TEACHER NOTES:
Keep notes brief - that is the modelling point.

[Stage: I Do | Find SDs]
33:
SOURCES:
- Storm Boy by Colin Thiele, page 62.

SAY:
- 'Watch this first. I am reading the extract and looking for details that show how the first man was rescued.'
- 'A man lashed himself in, and signalled to Hide-Away to start pulling on the thin rope. The rescue was ready to start.'
- 'I notice: the man tied himself in. He signalled. The rescue began.'
- 'Then: the sea sprang and snatched at the man on the rope like a beast with white teeth. The waves swept him under. Storm Boy could feel the shock and shudder of the line.'
- 'I notice: the waves were dangerous, the man was nearly pulled under, but he kept rising back up.'

DO:
- Click to reveal as you model.
- Underline or point to the details in the extract as you call them out.
- Note the use of shudder.

TEACHER NOTES:
Use a think-aloud to make your reading visible.

[Stage: I Do | Find SDs]
34:
SOURCES:
- Storm Boy by Colin Thiele, page 62.

SAY:
- 'Continuing the extract. Watch this first.'
- 'Hide-Away and Fingerbone pulled until their feet dug deep into the sand, and the muscles that stood out on their arms looked like the rope they were pulling.'
- 'I notice: Hide-Away and Fingerbone pulled with all their might.'
- 'Then they were able to haul the man through the thud and tug of the sea to the shore.'
- 'I notice: they hauled him to safety.'

DO:
- Click to reveal as you model.
- Mark the action verbs (pulled, hauled, dropped) on the board.

TEACHER NOTES:
Next slide turns these notes into the SPO.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who copy whole sentences; push to note form.

[Stage: I Do | Find SDs]
35:
SAY:
- 'Two options of supporting details. Which set matches the topic sentence?'
- 'TS: Thanks to Mr Percival, they were able to work as a team to finally rescue the first man from the rickety boat.'
- 'Option A: Waves are powerful. Boat stuck. Stormy day at sea.'
- 'Option B: Waves pull at him - swept under. Hide-Away and Fingerbone pulled with might. Haul man to shore.'
- Ask: 'A or B on your fingers. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: B.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why is option B better?' Expected: 'A is about the setting. B is about the rescue.'

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers A or B
Script:
- 'Which set matches the topic sentence? Show me.'
- Scan for: clear majority on B.
PROCEED:
- Confirm B; supporting details support the topic, not just the setting.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students pick A because it sounds dramatic.
- Reteach with the rule: 'Read the topic sentence again. It is about the rescue. Pick details that show the rescue.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who think every detail is a supporting detail.

[Stage: CFU | SPO]
36:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first. I am adding the supporting details to my SPO.'
- 'SD1: Waves pull at him - swept under.'
- 'SD2: Hide-Away and Fingerbone pulled with might.'
- 'SD3: Haul man to shore.'
- 'Notice they are in note form, not full sentences.'

DO:
- Click to reveal each detail as you say it.
- Point to the abbreviations and symbols.

TEACHER NOTES:
The note form is unpacked into full sentences in lesson 20.

[Stage: I Do | SPO Build]
37:
SAY:
- 'Now we add a concluding sentence.'
- 'Remember: it summarises and echoes the topic without repeating it.'
- 'Whiteboards. Try a concluding sentence for this SPO. One minute.'
- 'Three, two, one, show.'
- 'I will reveal an example.'

DO:
- Circulate; read several boards.
- Reveal: 'Finally on dry land, he was shivering and exhausted, but he was safe.'
- Discuss why it works: it summarises without repeating the topic sentence.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who copy the topic sentence; remind them to echo, not copy.

[Stage: We Do | CS]
38:
SAY:
- 'When writing a concluding sentence, which option is best?'
- 'One: copy the topic sentence word for word.'
- 'Two: introduce a new idea.'
- 'Three: write it in note form.'
- 'Four: echo the ideas of the topic sentence, but in different words.'
- Ask: 'Show me one, two, three or four. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 4.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why not option 1?' Expected: 'because then the paragraph just repeats itself.'

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers 1-4
Script:
- 'Show me which option a concluding sentence should do.'
- Scan for: clear majority on 4.
PROCEED:
- Confirm 4.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students pick 1 because they think echoing means copying.
- Reteach with the metaphor: 'Echo bounces back the same idea, in different words.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick 3 (note form); the CS is a full sentence.

[Stage: CFU | CS]
39:
SAY:
- 'Now we will do an SPO together. The main idea is: Mr Percival takes the line to the boat.'
- 'I will read the extract from pages 59 and 60. We will find supporting details together.'

DO:
- Frame the task.
- Point to the main idea.

TEACHER NOTES:
Main idea sentence is given. Students need to find SDs from the text.

[Stage: We Do | SPO]
40:
SOURCES:
- Storm Boy by Colin Thiele, pages 59 to 60.

SAY:
- 'Read the extract with me.'
- 'Out to the boat, out to the boat, they all shouted. But Mr Percival did not understand. He flew too far to one side, dropped the line in the sea, and turned back. Missed, said Hide-Away. But it was a good try, said Storm Boy.'
- 'Then: this time Mr Percival flew straight towards the boat but did not go quite far enough.'
- Ask: 'On your whiteboards, jot one detail in note form. What happened on the first attempts? Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Choral read first.
- Click to reveal.
- Scan boards. Look for notes like 'first try - too far one side, missed', 'second try - not far enough'.
- Cold call two students.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who copy whole lines; redirect to short notes.

[Stage: We Do | SPO]
41:
SOURCES:
- Storm Boy by Colin Thiele, pages 59 to 60.

SAY:
- 'Continuing the extract.'
- 'He held Mr Percival like a big duck and gave him another piece of fish. Again and again they tried, and again and again they missed.'
- 'Storm Boy and Hide-Away were disappointed but they did not give up. Neither did Mr Percival. He flew out and back, out and back, until at last, on the tenth try, he did it. A great gust of wind suddenly lifted him up and flung him sideways. He threw up his big wing and just as he banked sharply over the tugboat, dropped the line. It fell right across the drowning ship.'
- Ask: 'On your whiteboards, jot a note for what changed on the tenth try. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Choral read first.
- Click to reveal.
- Scan boards. Look for 'tenth try - gust of wind, dropped line on ship'.
- Cold call two students.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who write 'they did it' with no detail; push for the how.

[Stage: We Do | SPO]
42:
SAY:
- 'Three supporting details. Drag them into the right order on your whiteboard.'
- 'Countless tries no luck never give up. First Mr P took line too far missed. Tenth try success.'
- Ask: 'Three, two, one, show.' Expected: first, countless, tenth.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why is this the right order?'

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Whiteboard Show
Script:
- 'Show me the order.'
- Scan for: 80% have the correct sequence.
PROCEED:
- Move to the SPO build.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students start with success because it sounds important.
- Reteach with the rule: 'Time order tells the story. First, then, finally. The tenth try is finally.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who do not consider chronology.

[Stage: CFU | SPO Order]
43:
SAY:
- 'On your whiteboards, list the supporting details in note form.'
- 'Use the three we just sorted. Add them to the SPO frame.'
- 'Three minutes.'

DO:
- Circulate; read several boards.
- Cold call one student to read theirs.

WATCH FOR:
- Students writing full sentences; redirect to note form.

[Stage: We Do | SPO Build]
44:
SAY:
- 'Now we add the topic sentence.'
- 'Whiteboards. Try one yourself first. The main idea is: Mr Percival takes the line to the boat.'
- 'When I click, an option will appear. Yours can be different.'

DO:
- Circulate; read several boards.
- Reveal: 'Mr Percival, an expert at fetch-the-pebble, was the fishermen's only hope.'
- Cold call non-volunteers to share theirs.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who copy the main idea; push for a richer topic sentence.

[Stage: We Do | TS]
45:
SAY:
- 'Last step. Add a concluding sentence.'
- 'Echo the topic, do not repeat. Keep it brief.'
- 'Whiteboards. Three minutes.'
- 'When I click, an example will appear.'

DO:
- Circulate; read several boards.
- Reveal: 'Thanks to Mr Percival's perseverance, they were finally ready to start their rescue.'
- Discuss why it echoes without repeating.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who repeat the topic sentence.

[Stage: We Do | CS]
46:
SAY:
- 'Read the SPO. Does this concluding sentence accurately complete it?'
- 'TS: The captain, who is eternally grateful for Storm Boy's help, offers a deal.'
- 'CS: The captain, desperate to help Storm Boy, leaves his offer on the table if they change their mind.'
- Ask: 'Thumbs up if it works, thumbs down if not. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan thumbs.
- Ask: 'Why does this CS work?' Expected: 'It echoes the captain's offer without repeating the topic sentence.'

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Thumbs Up or Down
Script:
- 'Does this CS work? Thumbs up or down.'
- Scan for: clear majority on thumbs up.
PROCEED:
- Confirm; this CS echoes the captain's offer without repeating the TS.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students think any sentence about the captain works.
- Reteach with the rule: 'A CS has to summarise the SDs as well as echo the TS.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who say thumbs up without checking against the SDs.

[Stage: CFU | CS]
47:
SAY:
- 'Independent work. Complete this SPO.'
- 'TS and CS are given. You add SD2 and SD3 about how the crew were saved.'
- 'Use your novel and your notes from earlier.'

DO:
- Set timer.
- Circulate; check first 2 to 3 SDs per student.
- This slide may be hidden by default - unhide if your class needs scaffolding.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: provide three or four phrase options for SD2 and SD3 to choose from.
- Extra Notes: pair with a partner.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: write a fresh SPO with their own TS for a different section of the story.

TEACHER NOTES:
Skip if the class can move straight to the booklet.

WATCH FOR:
- SDs that do not match the TS.

[Stage: You Do | Optional Scaffold]
48:
SAY:
- 'Open your booklet to Lesson 17 Sentence Level Writing.'
- 'Complete the SPO tasks. Use the four parts: TS, three SDs in note form, CS.'
- 'Until the closing.'

DO:
- Set timer.
- Circulate; read first 2 to 3 SDs per student.
- Pull a small group for re-modelling on TS or CS.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: provide a topic sentence and a concluding sentence; students fill in just the SDs.
- Extra Notes: pair with a peer.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: write two SPOs for two different sections. Compare which TS works best.

TEACHER NOTES:
The booklet is the You Do for the SPO objective.

WATCH FOR:
- Off-topic SDs.
- CS that just repeats the TS.
- SDs as full sentences instead of notes.

[Stage: You Do | Booklet]
